comparator.name: Scandinavian Languages and Cultures (Scandinavia Studies)
comparator.academicYear: Current published UvA bachelor curriculum, checked 2026-09-27
comparator.sourceNotes: The official programme is 60+60+60=180 EC. The generic target requires one of three main-language routes; Danish is selected by the official-order tie-break, independently of UCR fit. Year 1 totals 60 EC and includes four successive main-language proficiency courses, Scandinavian languages and Viking-world study, and humanities and regional-studies foundations. Year 2 totals 60 EC: 30 EC of literature, science philosophy, European literary classics, advanced language proficiency and a sociolinguistics research project, plus a 30-EC Scandinavian-study-abroad block in the published table. The page's narrative recommends but does not require study abroad and later refers to it as a third-year option, while the table places the 30-EC block in year 2; the reconstruction preserves the table's credit-bearing block without inventing host courses and notes that students may arrange a non-abroad substitute. Year 3 totals 60 EC: three 6-EC courses, 30 EC genuine free choice and a 12-EC graduation project. The programme develops high proficiency in the selected main language and passive proficiency in the other two Scandinavian languages.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target names no main language. The current official programme page presents Danish first in its list of the three main-language choices, before Norwegian and Swedish, so Danish is selected as a neutral tie-break without reference to UCR fit. The programme still includes passive study of the other two Scandinavian languages.

exception.reason: The defining curriculum requires five successive main-language proficiency courses, main-language-specific literature and translation, passive proficiency in the other two Scandinavian languages, and a sustained Scandinavian languages, literature, history, identity and sociolinguistics sequence. The current UCR catalogue offers no Danish, Norwegian or Swedish language instruction and no Scandinavian-language reading, writing, speaking or translation sequence. A 24-course programme assembled from general literature, communication, politics, history and cultural study would replace the compulsory language-acquisition and Scandinavian area-studies core rather than provide a defensible closest UCR match. The 30 EC of genuine open choice cannot compensate for the missing compulsory language progression.
exception.curriculumContext: The selected Danish full-time route totals exactly 180 EC: 60 EC in year one, 60 EC in year two and 60 EC in year three. It contains four successive 6-EC Danish proficiency courses in year one, a fifth advanced proficiency course in year two, Danish-specific literature and translation, comparative Scandinavian-language study, regional cultural-history courses, a sociolinguistics research project and a Scandinavian-studies graduation project. The public page's table places a 30-EC Scandinavian study-abroad component in year two, while its narrative recommends but does not require study abroad and later describes it as a third-year possibility. The reconstruction preserves the published 30-EC block and does not invent host or replacement courses; the exception rests on the missing Scandinavian-language disciplinary core, not on this presentation inconsistency.
exception.ucrCourseEvidence: Reviewed all 151 rows of the current enriched UCR course workbook, including course names, descriptions, outline-derived profiles, prerequisites, planned availability and topics. MCCLITR211 World Myth & Literature includes Norse myth within a global comparative course, but does not teach Scandinavian language, literature or area studies. HCBCOGN312 Psycholinguistics studies neurobiological and psychological mechanisms of language acquisition, comprehension and production; MCCCOMM211 Style & Meaning studies linguistic choices and stylistics in mostly English-language texts; neither is a language-acquisition course. GOSPOLI112 Foundations of Comparative Politics mentions Sweden only as an example within a global comparison of political systems. General literature, history, political science and communication courses provide adjacent methods but no sustained Scandinavian focus. None of the 151 courses teaches Danish, Norwegian or Swedish grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, speaking, writing, reading or translation, and none supplies a Scandinavian sociolinguistics or modern Nordic regional sequence. The workbook therefore provides no defensible basis for a scheduled 24-course UCR Scandinavian Languages and Cultures programme.
